### Problem: Max points on a line {#sec-lang-p6-points}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $n \le 300$ distinct points with integer coordinates ($|x|, |y| \le 10^4$), return the maximum number of points that lie on one straight line.

Source: [LC 149 · Max Points on a Line](https://leetcode.com/problems/max-points-on-a-line/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Fix an anchor point; two other points are on the same line through it iff their direction vectors from the anchor are parallel. Store each direction as a **reduced integer pair** $(dx/g, dy/g)$ with a fixed sign, never as the float $dy/dx$: floats break on vertical lines, and with large coordinates two different slopes can round to the same double.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** For each pair $(i, j)$, count points $k$ with zero cross product $(p_j - p_i) \times (p_k - p_i) = 0$: $O(n^3)$, $2.7\cdot10^7$ for $n = 300$.
2. **Hash directions per anchor.** For each $i$, for each $j > i$: $(dx, dy) = p_j - p_i$, divide by $g = \gcd(dx, dy)$, and make the pair canonical ($dx > 0$, or $dx = 0$ and $dy > 0$). Count equal pairs; the best line through $i$ has $1 + \max$ count points.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: lang-points
def max_points(points):
    n, best = len(points), min(len(points), 2)
    for i in range(n):
        x1, y1 = points[i]
        dirs = Counter()
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            dx, dy = points[j][0] - x1, points[j][1] - y1
            g = math.gcd(dx, dy)                   # > 0 because the points are distinct
            dx, dy = dx // g, dy // g
            if dx < 0 or (dx == 0 and dy < 0):
                dx, dy = -dx, -dy
            dirs[(dx, dy)] += 1
            best = max(best, 1 + dirs[(dx, dy)])
    return best

def max_points_float(points):              # the tempting version with float slopes
    best = min(len(points), 2)
    for i, (x1, y1) in enumerate(points):
        slopes = Counter((y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) if x2 != x1 else math.inf for x2, y2 in points[i + 1 :])
        best = max([best] + [1 + c for c in slopes.values()])
    return best

def max_points_brute(points):
    n, best = len(points), min(len(points), 2)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            (x1, y1), (x2, y2) = points[i], points[j]
            best = max(best, sum((x2 - x1) * (y - y1) == (y2 - y1) * (x - x1) for x, y in points))
    return best

for _ in range(400):
    pts = random.sample([(x, y) for x in range(-3, 4) for y in range(-3, 4)], random.randint(1, 10))
    assert max_points(pts) == max_points_brute(pts)

assert max_points([(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)]) == 3
assert max_points([(1, 1), (3, 2), (5, 3), (4, 1), (2, 3), (1, 4)]) == 4
assert max_points([(0, 0)]) == 1
close_slopes = [(0, 0), (94911151, 94911150), (94911152, 94911151)]
assert max_points(close_slopes) == max_points_brute(close_slopes) == 2
assert max_points_float(close_slopes) == 3                   # two different slopes round to the same double
```

#### C++

```cpp
int gcdAbs(int a, int b) {                        // gcd of |a| and |b|, never negative
    a = abs(a); b = abs(b);
    while (b) { int t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

int maxPoints(const vector<vector<int>>& p) {
    int n = p.size(), best = min(n, 2);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        map<pair<int, int>, int> dirs;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j) {
            int dx = p[j][0] - p[i][0], dy = p[j][1] - p[i][1];
            int g = gcdAbs(dx, dy);                     // > 0 because the points are distinct
            dx /= g; dy /= g;
            if (dx < 0 || (dx == 0 && dy < 0)) { dx = -dx; dy = -dy; }
            best = max(best, 1 + ++dirs[{dx, dy}]);
        }
    }
    return best;
}
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
pts6 = [(1, 1), (3, 2), (5, 3), (4, 1), (2, 3), (1, 4)]
on_line = [q for q in pts6 if q[0] + q[1] == 5]
assert len(on_line) == max_points(pts6) == 4

def axes(ax, p):
    xs = np.linspace(0.5, 4.5, 2)
    ax.plot(xs, 5 - xs, color=p["green"], lw=1.5, ls="--")
    ax.scatter(*zip(*pts6), color=p["muted"], s=40, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(*zip(*on_line), color=p["green"], s=60, zorder=4)
    ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
V.plot(axes, size=(4.2, 3.0))
```

The second sample: four points on the line x + y = 5, found by the reduced direction (1, -1) from the anchor (1, 4).

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n^2 \log C)$ where $C$ bounds the coordinates (the gcd), with expected $O(1)$ hashing in Python and $O(\log n)$ `map` operations in C++. **Space** $O(n)$ per anchor.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$ or $2$: the answer is $n$.
- Vertical lines: $dx = 0$ is canonicalised to $(0, 1)$; the float version needs a special case.
- Without the sign rule, $(1, 2)$ and $(-1, -2)$ would count as different directions.
- If points could repeat, count duplicates of the anchor separately and add them to every line.
:::
